items.title: Waterloo Park Plan Update and Funding
notes: Release for 2026 Implementation
Report No.: COM2026-022
Prepared By: Anna lee Sangster
Anna lee Sangster gave a presentation outlining the general improvements made to the park after the 2009 Park Plan, as well as changes that were made through the implementation efforts.

Claire Basinski, Take Consulting Ltd. and Eliza Oprescu, MHBC gave a presentation outlining the plan for the workshop and for the Waterloo Park Plan project, including the timeline and themes for the planning phase.
They then facilitated the workshop, further outlining each of the themes and giving Council an opportunity to provide input.
Councillor Wright highlighted that waste management and managing invasive species should be included.
Councillor Roe mentioned that, as the READI Team liaison, accessible play components are very important, especially thinking about where an accessible swing would go and what it would look like.

Councillor Freeman talked about the difference between passive and recreational activation of space, as well as keeping programmed space separate, such as park rentals. On the programming piece, it is helpful to have an understanding of a needs assessment for the programmed recreational fields, as it ebbs and flows in pressure.

Councillor Hanmer expanded on what the other comments made, especially as far as recreational activation and programmed space, as it should be available as a drop in space. Accessibility of the spaces is also a key theme, as equipment and wayfinding may need to be updated. Planning to make spaces multi-use is also appreciated.

Councillor Bodaly started with thanking the Waterloo Park Advisory Committee for the substantive work they did to supplement this process. Adding on to what the other Councillors mentioned about recreational vs. programmed space, Councillor Bodaly also contributed that there is a tension because the City is running out of space for programs. It’s also important to make the spaces inviting and active for the general public when they’re not programmed. He also didn’t see arts space mentioned and would advocate for that to have its own theme.

Councillor Roach provided feedback that Waterloo Park should remain a city-wide park, not just for the Uptown or to be used as an events space. The park has to work for everyone, and he emphasized safety, maintenance, and practical year-round use as key themes. He supports investment in what is essential and urgent, such as safe paths, lighting, seating and accessible connections. He also highlighted the importance of a welcoming space that’s not over-programmed.

Councillor Vasic described balancing fiscal responsibility with enhancements to invest in, giving the example of separating cyclists and pedestrians as what works well. The park should be a place of tourism, and she didn’t see that element mentioned, as it brings people in for international tournaments and events like Lumen. She would like to see Waterloo Park as a beautiful, fully invested space in the centre of town, similar to a Central Park feel.

Mayor McCabe also highlighted arts spaces in the park, including planned events like the Waterloo Concert Band and their needs as far as electricity and storage space. She asked about pop-up or impromptu performances as well and how you make those work in the space. She wondered about connections to and from the park, and how to connect people across the City in ways that are easy and accessible to everyone regardless of age or ability. Mayor McCabe also asked if there were better uses of the Park Inn or Potters’ House.
Councillor Wright added that the project will likely be dollar constrained, so they should think about partnerships and opportunities, especially with the post secondary partners along the park.
Claire Basinski, Take Consulting Ltd. summarized the comments received during this section of the workshop.
Mayor McCabe added that accessibility is an important piece, and echoed Councillor Wright’s comments about the universities along the park, adding the importance of connections with them.

Councillor Freeman also noted the importance of arts of culture with the notion of balance. It would be important to see how commentary on the themes are being balanced within the plan. She emphasised Councillor Roach’s comments around how the park means a lot of things to a lot of people.

Councillor Vasic asked about next steps, as she won’t be on Council to see the plan come forward, and since not everything can be accomplished for Waterloo Park, maybe some features could be implemented when Bechtel Park comes forward for an update.
She also mentioned the Parkland Strategy which points to park safety, and that park ambassadors are worth thinking about.
Eliza Oprescu, MHBC outlined the next steps for engagement and the park plan. Claire Basinski, Take Consulting Ltd. then responded to questions of Council.

items.title: Zoning By-law Amendment Z-26-09
notes: City-Initiated (Housing Accelerator
Fund Initiative #9)
Prepared by: Brenna MacKinnon
Ward No.: City-Wide

Brenna MacKinnon gave a presentation outlining the proposed Zoning By-law Amendment, including how this proposed amendment came about and how the sites were selected, and other locations in the City where places of worship have built housing on site. Brenna MacKinnon then responded to questions of Council. Joel Cotter and Adam Lauder also responded to questions of Council.

Sheri Wolff, Resident of Waterloo spoke in favour of more housing, but against the proposed Zoning by-law amendment, especially in regard to Parkminster United Church due to issues with pedestrian safety and neighbourhood compatibility.

Manju Porwal, Director, Brason Montessori spoke about running operations at Parkminster United Church for the childcare centre, and their concerns over what might happen to the centre if the proposal goes through. Manju Porwal then responded to questions of Council.

Brian Schellenberg, Member, The Church of God (German) spoke in opposition to the proposed zone change, especially when the property owners did not request it, as there have been no site-specific studies done to the properties. Brian Schellenberg then responded to questions of Council.
Karen Noble, Resident of Waterloo spoke against in opposition to the proposed zone change for The Church of God, citing neighbourhood incompatibility and climate change concerns.

Mary Ehnis, Resident of Waterloo spoke about the legal concerns with the proposed zone change, including the notice given to residents regarding the proposal, the water constraints in the Region, and the lack of studies for the sites. Mary Ehnis then responded to questions of Council.
Charles Bye, Resident of Waterloo spoke about what the area means to their family and the neighbourhood, and against the proposed zone change.
Kirstie Allan, Resident of Waterloo spoke about the vibrancy of the Westvale neighbourhood, and against the proposed rezoning.
Michael Radivoi, Resident of Waterloo spoke about concerns with blanket upzoning, citing conflicts with the Official Plan, especially regarding 170 Middlebury Drive.

Stephanie Evans, Resident of Waterloo spoke in opposition to the proposed rezoning, as well as the work done to notify the neighbourhood of the proposed rezoning with the issues with the public notice. Stephanie Evans then responded to questions of Council.

Emi Bye Kondo, Resident of Waterloo spoke in opposition to the rezoning of places of worship, specifically regarding 170 Middlebury Drive, and spoke about living in the Westvale community. Emi Bye Kondo then responded to questions of Council.
Darryl O'Neill, Resident of Waterloo spoke about the changes to the neighbourhood and the removal of green spaces to build housing, especially regarding 170 Middlebury Drive.

Craig Sloss, Resident of Waterloo spoke about the need for more housing, especially affordable and sustainable housing, as well as more third spaces for communities. Craig Sloss then responded to questions of Council.
Shaun Booth, Resident of Waterloo spoke about considering the wishes of the Churches up for rezoning.
Heidi Ruttinger, Resident of Waterloo spoke about the need for affordable housing, but against the proposed rezoning of 170 Middlebury Drive as it would lead to the loss of green space and community.
Wendy Ridgway, Resident of Waterloo spoke about the experience with 250 Lincoln Road, and against the rezoning.
As no one else was present to speak to the application, the Chair concluded the Informal Public Meeting and indicated that staff will review the issues and report back to Council at a later date.
Brenna MacKinnon, Joel Cotter and Adam Lauder responded to questions of Council.

motions.text: WHEREAS the Province of Ontario’s Bill 60, Fighting Delays, Building Faster Act, 2025 was passed in November of 2025; and WHEREAS Schedule 16 of Bill 60 enacts the Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act, 2025; and WHEREAS the Act allows the Province to designate water corporations to manage water and wastewater services; and WHEREAS the Province has now enacted legislative amendments through Bill 98 to reinforce 100 per cent public sector ownership of water and wastewater public corporations, which reflects an important step in addressing concerns regarding ownership structures; and while the City recognizes this commitment, it remains important that the implementation of any such model continues to support strong municipal oversight, transparency, accountability, rate setting authority, asset stewardship, and long term integrated planning; and WHEREAS the Region of Waterloo has a lengthy history of managing our water and wastewater system, governed within a robust regulatory framework; and WHEREAS the current water capacity challenges within the Region of Waterloo underscore how foundational water security is to growth management, housing, economic stability and climate resilience within the Region; and WHEREAS Regional decision making, rate setting and governance are transparently governed by open meeting rules, allowing for complete public engagement; and WHEREAS the City of Waterloo is ultimately responsible for the local distribution and delivery of water to end users. THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the City of Waterloo affirms its support for the continued public ownership and governance of drinking water and wastewater services, recognizing water as essential to public health, environmental protection, and long-term community well-being; and BE IT RESOLVED that the City of Waterloo encourages the Province of Ontario to review Schedule 16 of Bill 60 through a lens of public health and system resilience, groundwater protection and long-term water security, governance, accountability, and transparency financial sustainability, and affordability, planning, growth management, and climate adaptation; and BE IT RESOLVED that the City of Waterloo encourages the Province of Ontario to enact and maintain explicit statutory protections requiring public-sector ownership of water and wastewater corporations, including prohibitions on private share ownership or transfer; and BE IT RESOLVED that a copy of this resolution be sent to the Premier of Ontario, the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, to local and area MPP’s, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, the Ontario Big City Mayors, and to the Region of Waterloo and local area municipalities.
